issue_context.body:
from @eerhardt in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/82179#discussion_r1131513910 (fyi @stephentoub)

> A couple things here:
> 
> Parsing:
> 
> 1. In order to be consistent with the reflection based behavior, we need to catch the int.Parse exception thrown here, and wrap it in a `InvalidOperationException` and add the configuration path of the invalid data. This allows devs to easily know where the invalid data exists from the exception message.
> 2. This should be `int.Parse(valueString, NumberStyles.Integer, NumberFormatInfo.InvariantInfo);`
> 
> See the following for how I did it when manually writing the bind code for Console Logging:
> 
> https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/967250cc86b4c613015066b47b882e7424fdb590/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Console/src/ConsoleLoggerOptions.cs#L222-L239

If we decide to directly use converters we should measure the size impact -- maybe directly referencing a converter is less expensive then GetCoverter (which I think @eerhardt said is huge), but it still looks pretty big.  Maybe we can just look to the converters for inspiration of which parse/tryparse signatures to call, then generate those?
I think the idea is not using the converters at all and just having the parse code embedded inside the generated code. no dependency and not calling type converter.

For built-in types like `int`, `bool`, and `enum`, I don't see a benefit pulling TypeConverter into the app. Using the parsing logic directly makes sense to me.

See also https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/44493#issuecomment-1425969210 about TypeConverter extensibility being opt-in.

The one use of config binding in Console Logging shouldn't pull in TypeConverter at all. See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/81931 for why and numbers.

> I think the idea is not using the converters at all and just having the parse code embedded inside the generated code. no dependency and not calling type converter.

Yeah this is what I meant.

@tarekgh @eerhardt I'm using the list of "intrinsic" types specified in the core `TypeConverter` assembly to determine which primitives need support - https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/967250cc86b4c613015066b47b882e7424fdb590/src/libraries/System.ComponentModel.TypeConverter/src/System/ComponentModel/ReflectTypeDescriptionProvider.cs#L162-L198

Are there any other strategies for picking these types that come to mind?
I think the collected list of primitives is good enough and we can watch if we get more cases we need to support.

Looking at:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/bd6ed47fb8836556db3a0f792b4c432cf5a65d4e/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder/src/ConfigurationBinder.cs#L838-L873

I think starting with those built-in Types makes a lot of sense, as those will be the types that can be converted out of the box with `TypeDescriptor.GetConverter(type)`. Note you will only need the Types that have a TypeConverter that `CanConvertFrom(typeof(string)) == true`.

1. Looks like `Nullable<>` should be tested to ensure it works correctly.
2. The last Type to consider would be `byte[]`, since it is built directly into ConfigurationBinder.

> Looks like Nullable<> should be tested to ensure it works correctly.
> The last Type to consider would be byte[], since it is built directly into ConfigurationBinder.

Yup we already have tests for these two; will just doublecheck that the implementation lines up with reflection in all cases.

review_comments:
>Int128 [](http://example.com/codeflow?start=37&length=6)

What about the other numeric types? like int, uint, long, ulong...etc?

Those types are ["special"](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.specialtype?view=roslyn-dotnet) in Roslyn APIs, so we can do type checks based on `ITypeSymbol.SpecialType`. I'll add a comment.

What about all the other types that TypeConverter supports in the box?

[https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/5711ca33f8dd1758e18c09ebdedf7e95eb424e0f/src/libraries/System.ComponentModel.TypeConverter/src/System/ComponentModel/ReflectTypeDescriptionProvider.cs#L164-L191](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/5711ca33f8dd1758e18c09ebdedf7e95eb424e0f/src/libraries/System.ComponentModel.TypeConverter/src/System/ComponentModel/ReflectTypeDescriptionProvider.cs#L164-L191)

Guid, Version, Date/Time types, float, double, etc.
I am seeing these types are supported in the parser. I agree will be good to add them to the test here too. good idea!

There are unit tests for all of the types in question.

For the baseline tests, I cherry-picked representative types that cover all the parsing schemes used in the emitter. But yeah I'll add all of them to catch regressions.
